Score tests for relaxing a fitted model

Source: R/ctScoreTest.R
ctScoreTest.Rd

Tests, from one fitted model and without refitting it, whether the model would fit better if it were relaxed: parameters that differ between subjects (a missing random effect), parameters that depend on a time independent covariate the model does not include, or dynamics that depend on the latent state (a missing nonlinearity). Each test is a score (Lagrange multiplier) test: the slope of the log likelihood in the direction of the relaxation, at the fitted model, with the fitted parameters projected out. Each also gives a one-step estimate of the size of the relaxation. These estimates are for screening, so refit with the relaxations that matter before interpreting their sizes.

Usage

ctScoreTest(
  fit,
  covariates = NULL,
  tests = c("heterogeneity", "covariates", "statedependence", "volatility", "fixed",
    "level", "instability"),
  form = c("auto", "linear", "spline", "factor", "threshold"),
  df = 3,
  parameters = NULL,
  order = 2L,
  variance = c("robust", "model"),
  nboot = 1999L,
  exact = 5L,
  intoverpop = c("laplace", "quadrature"),
  cores = getOption("mc.cores", 2L),
  verbose = TRUE
)

Arguments

fit

An optimised fit from ctFit with backend = 'julia'.

covariates

Optional data frame of subject level covariates to test, with a column named as the fit's subject id (or id) and one column per covariate. Long data with repeated rows per subject can be used if each covariate is constant within subject. Without an id column, give one row per subject in the fit's subject order.

tests

Which families to run: any of 'heterogeneity', 'covariates', 'statedependence', 'volatility', 'fixed', 'level' and 'instability'. By default all but 'instability'. Covariates are tested only when covariates is given or 'covariates' is asked for (then the model's own predictors alone), and levels only where the model has a random intercept.

form

How a covariate enters: 'auto' (indicators for a factor, character or logical covariate, linear otherwise), 'linear', 'spline', 'factor' or 'threshold' (a step at an unknown cut). One value, or one per covariate.

df

Degrees of freedom of the spline basis.

parameters

Optional parameter names to restrict the heterogeneity and covariate tests to.

order

Highest degree of the state dependence terms. 2 tests each drift coefficient varying linearly with each state. 3 adds variation with products and squares of states, which is needed to see a symmetric dependence, such as regulation that strengthens at both extremes.

variance

'robust' (the default) or 'model'; see the section on variance.

nboot

Bootstrap resamples for the robust p-values.

exact

For statedependence, volatility and fixed with the robust variance: how many of each family's terms are corrected exactly for the estimation of the fitted parameters, which takes two evaluations of the extended model per term. Every term is first tested without that correction, which is conservative, and the strongest exact terms are then corrected (projected in the tables). Inf corrects every term.

intoverpop

How the extended families (statedependence, volatility, fixed, level) integrate the random effects on a Laplace fit. 'laplace' (the default) uses the Laplace approximation, a fast screen. 'quadrature' integrates every subject's random effects by quadrature, as ctFit(intoverpop = 'quadrature') does, which removes the Laplace error from these families and takes longer. The other families use the fit's own objective either way.

cores

Engine cores for the evaluations.

verbose

Report progress.

Value

An object of class ctScoreTest, a list with heterogeneity (a data frame, one row per parameter or fixed MANIFESTMEANS cell), dimension (the largest eigenvalue, its p-value and the direction, when two or more parameters are tested), blocks (on a reduced rank level, dimension, a row per block with the one-step sd along its direction, covariance, a row per pair of blocks, and directions, the direction found for each tested block), covariates (one element per covariate, each a list of its joint test and a data frame parameters, including the model's own predictors, marked by joint$inmodel), statedependence (a list of terms, a data frame, and joint, the tests per equation and overall), volatility (the same, for the innovation sds), fixed (a list of cells, their joint test, and untested, cells that could not be tested and why), instability (a list of parameters, one row per ordering and parameter, and joint, per ordering), and info (how the fit integrated its random effects, the number of subjects and parameters, the variance used, and errors, why any family was not tested). Tables have a class column where relaxations are alike, and the extended families a projected column, whether a term was corrected exactly (see exact).

Heterogeneity

Tests letting each parameter vary over subjects, as ctFit would fit it, for each free parameter that does not vary already and is not an initial condition (T0MEANS and T0VAR). The test covers the parameter's variance over subjects together with its covariances with what already varies: each subject's initial state (the free T0MEANS parameters) and the parameters with random effects, listed in with. Even a model without random effects has initial states, so these covariances are tested there too. They matter because a varying CINT intercept that is unrelated to the initial means makes subjects drift apart from a common start, while the same intercept correlated with each subject's start is a random intercept.

The covariances are tested as ordinary score tests, and the variance, given them, as a one sided test (Stram & Lee, 1994), so LM is referred to an equal mixture of chi-square distributions on df - 1 and df degrees of freedom. z is the one sided test of the variance alone, with its covariances held at zero, which has more power when the new effect is independent of what already varies. p is the smaller of the two tests' p-values, calibrated by resampling subjects. A negative z beside a large LM means the parameter varies only together with what already varies, as an intercept does with each subject's start. No assumption is made about how the initial states relate to the dynamics.

The statistic is the information matrix test, which is the score test for neglected heterogeneity (Chesher, 1984). Other misspecification can also move it. A drift that varies over subjects also moves the diffusion's test, for example, and a missing nonlinearity moves several. sd is the one-step estimate of the subjects' standard deviation on the raw scale, with the covariances estimated alongside, and sd_natural approximately the same on the parameter's own scale. They are NA where the test comes from the covariances and the variance alone is estimated as zero, as often happens for an intercept, and then only a refit can give the size. To act on a result, set indvarying = TRUE for the parameter and the T0MEANS parameters, refit, and test again. ctModelImprove does this.

Each MANIFESTMEANS cell the model fixes is also tested, as a random intercept on that indicator around its fixed value (rows named MANIFESTMEANS[...]). With one indicator per latent this overlaps with the covariances of the CINT rows, with more indicators it is the indicator's own intercept, and for a latent with no free intercept it is the only test of its level. To act on it, give the cell a parameter with the fixed value as its stated mean (ctPar(mean=)) and indvarying = TRUE.

On a reduced rank level (poprank), a parameter that varies only through the shared dimensions, without a variance of its own, is tested for variation outside those dimensions. Each such test is of the variance alone. A parameter whose test is already determined by the fitted model, as for an intercept that loads on the shared dimensions, is not tested (NA) and is left out of dimension.

dimension tests whether subjects vary along some combination of the tested parameters, a new dimension of variation, with its covariances with what already varies held at zero. The statistic is the largest eigenvalue of the standardised score matrix of the variances, tested against a bootstrap over subjects, and its eigenvector gives the direction, as relative loadings on the raw scale. It can detect variation spread over several parameters that no single test picks up, and is less sensitive than the best single test when one parameter carries it. It is not computed over a reduced rank level's parameters, whose blocks are tested instead.

On a reduced rank level, blocks tests what its blocks of shared dimensions (popblocks, or without them the whole level as one block) leave out, beside the own variances. blocks$dimension tests, within each block with more effects than dimensions, whether the block needs another shared dimension, with the block's fitted loadings projected out. The rows for single parameters, which test own variances, cannot show this. blocks$covariance tests, for each pair of blocks, the covariances between their dimensions, which the model holds at zero, with a joint two sided score test. An example is whether a response style shared by an item's thresholds covaries with the dynamic level. A pair in which one block loads on every effect of the other already has these covariances in the model, and is listed with a note but not tested. Both are calibrated by resampling subjects and adjusted together (p_adj). An effect whose population mean is stated is tested through the model with that mean free and set to its stated value, and only the fit's own parameters are projected out. ctModelImprove acts on both, adding a dimension to a block or letting blocks share dimensions.

Covariates

For each covariate, tests the effects it would have on every tested parameter if it were added as a time independent predictor (on the raw scale), including effects on the population standard deviations of the parameters that vary. The joint test of all of a covariate's effects is the screen. For each parameter, estimate is the one-step effect per unit of the covariate, estimated jointly over the parameters with the other fitted parameters held at their estimates, so that a covariate that shifts one parameter is not attributed to another that is correlated with it. Holding the other parameters keeps the estimate close to what a refit would give. estimate_natural gives it approximately on the parameter's own scale, and p tests it. A covariate enters linearly (centred), as treatment indicators for a factor, or as a natural spline with df degrees of freedom, for which only p is given. Subjects with a missing value contribute at the mean. To act on a result, add the covariate to the data and to TIpredNames, and refit.

The model's own time independent predictors are tested as well, each on the parameters it does not yet act on, using the values the fit read. Their results have joint$inmodel set to TRUE. A predictor added with an effect on one parameter may act on another too, and that can show only once other changes are made. To act on a result, set the predictor's effect on that parameter (<predictor>_effect in model$pars) and refit. ctModelImprove does that.

form = 'threshold' tests for a step at an unknown cut instead. The joint test is computed at each cut from the 15th to the 85th percentile, and the largest (Andrews, 1993), which is the split a score based tree makes, is compared with the same scan with the covariate permuted over subjects (Hothorn & Lausen, 2003). This accounts for the search and needs no refitting. The effects reported are those of being above the best cut, given as cut in the joint row.

On a reduced rank level, a covariate's effect on the spread of a varying parameter is tested as a scaling of that parameter's loadings and own sd together, reported as scale(<parameter>): the effect on its log standard deviation per unit of the covariate, with the correlations held fixed. With about 100 subjects these rows reject a correct model somewhat too often (6.5 to 8 per cent at .05), so read them only once the covariate's joint test has picked it out.

State dependence

For each latent equation and each pair of latent states k <= m, tests a term d * eta_k * eta_m in that equation's drift, that is, a drift coefficient that varies linearly with a state (Luukkonen, Saikkonen & Terasvirta, 1988). A term eta_k * eta_m in the equation of eta_i is DRIFT[i,k] varying with eta_m, or when k != m equally DRIFT[i,m] varying with eta_k. The data cannot tell these apart, and reads gives both. estimate is the one-step change in that drift coefficient per unit of the state. It is NA when the fitted model cannot size the term, which happens when the departure is strong, and the test itself is still valid. order = 3 adds the terms of degree three. The terms use the state predicted from earlier observations, as the filter does. To act on a result, write the dependence into the drift cell, for example DRIFT[1,1] = 'dr11 + d * eta2' with PARS = c('dr11|-log1p_exp(-param)', 'd'), and refit.

Volatility

tests = 'volatility' tests whether the size of each latent's innovations depends on a state, by scaling DIFFUSION[i, i], the innovation sd, by exp(v * eta_m) and testing v = 0, for every latent with innovations and every state. Variance that rises with a process's own level, as when negative affect is more variable when high, is the diagonal term. As for state dependence, the predicted state is used. To act on a result, write the scaling into the cell, for example DIFFUSION[2,2] = 'sd2 * exp(v * eta2)' with PARS = c('sd2|log1p_exp(param)', 'v'), and refit. ctModelImprove does this. These terms make the model nonlinear, so the test and a refit use the extended Kalman filter.

Level

tests = 'level' tests whether a parameter of the dynamics or of the error variances depends on a subject's level, where the level is a random intercept. For each free DRIFT, DIFFUSION and MANIFESTVAR parameter that does not vary over subjects, including a PARS parameter that those matrices read in an expression, and each MANIFESTMEANS or CINT intercept that does, it tests a term g * intercept added to the parameter, at g = 0, wherever the model reads the parameter. When subjects' levels are in the intercepts, the latent states are deviations from them, so the state dependence and volatility tests only see dependence on the deviation. A parameter that depends on a subject's usual level, such as persistence or innovation size that differs between people who are usually high and those usually low, otherwise shows only as heterogeneity, with no direction. These terms test that direction. The score is taken from the extended model's gradient, averaged over each subject's posterior for the intercept. estimate is the one-step change in the parameter, on its own scale, per unit of the intercept. To act on a result, let the parameter vary over subjects, so its correlation with the intercept is estimated. ctModelImprove does this. A model with no random intercept has nothing to test.

Fixed cells

For each cell the model fixes at zero that could sensibly be freed (a DRIFT cross effect, a DIFFUSION or MANIFESTVAR covariance between two that have a variance, a LAMBDA cross loading, a TDPREDEFFECT), tests freeing it. This is the modification index (Sorbom, 1989), and estimate is the expected parameter change. CINT and MANIFESTMEANS are not offered, since with the other one free, either is identified only through the initial transient. Under covmattransform = 'z', a covariance fixed at zero between variables that other covariances connect is held at zero by solving its cell. It is freed from that solved value (at in cells), and estimate is the change from it. If the solved value differs between subjects, because a covariance it depends on has random or predictor effects, the cell is not tested and is listed in untested. State dependence, volatility and fixed cells are tested on one extended model, so asking for several costs one preparation. If that model cannot be built, each family is tested separately.

Stability

tests = 'instability', run only when asked for, tests whether each parameter is stable across the data, with the data ordered by time, and by each latent's state as predicted from earlier observations. It uses each data row's score, whose partial sums behave as a Brownian bridge under the model (Nyblom, 1989). A parameter that changes over the study, or differs at high and low levels of a state, bends them. Ordered by a state, this is a test of state dependence of any form. The p-values come from a wild bootstrap over rows. It can take a long time on large data.

Alike relaxations

Two relaxations whose contributions from each subject are nearly collinear (correlation of 0.9 or more) would explain the same signal, and the data cannot tell them apart (MacCallum et al., 1993). They share a letter in class, and NA means alike to none. Refit with the most plausible one, then test again.

Variance and p-values

By default (variance = 'robust') the variance of each test is the spread over subjects of their projected contributions, and its p-value comes from a bootstrap over subjects of the studentised statistic (nboot resamples, from a fixed random stream, so a call is reproducible and leaves the session's random numbers alone). This keeps each test valid when the model is wrong in other ways. variance = 'model' uses the fitted model's curvature for the variance and chi-square and normal reference distributions. It is always used with fewer than 20 subjects.

Reading the results

The tests are screens. A badly misspecified model shows many significant tests at once, and the one-step sizes are local approximations, especially for drift parameters. Relax what stands out most, refit, and test again. Within each family p_adj is the Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment over the tests shown.

The tests use the fit's own objective, so they are for the intoverpop it was fitted with. They need an optimised fit, and refuse a sampled one. Heterogeneity and covariate tests need subjects as the independent units, so a model with a level above the subject can only be tested for state dependence. If a family cannot be tested on a model, the reason is given as a warning and in info$errors, and the other families' results stand. With priors = TRUE, the new terms are tested on the likelihood, without a prior.

On a Laplace fit with random dynamics beside random intercepts, the state dependence and volatility families use the one-step Laplace approximation for both the fit and its extension (see optimcontrol$laplace_onestep in ctFit). This is a fast screen whose approximation error stays in the scores, and info$onestep names the families concerned. intoverpop = 'quadrature' integrates every subject's random effects for these families instead (info$quadrature).

See also

vignette('score-tests') for three worked examples.

Examples

# \donttest{
if (isTRUE(ctJuliaStatus()$available)) {
# A model in which the innovations of the two processes are uncorrelated,
# with the DIFFUSION cell between them fixed at zero.
model <- ctModel(LAMBDA = diag(2),
  manifestNames = c('Y1', 'Y2'), latentNames = c('eta1', 'eta2'),
  TDpredNames = 'TD1',
  DIFFUSION = matrix(c('diff_eta1', 0, 0, 'diff_eta2'), 2, 2))
fit <- ctFit(ctsemtestdat, model, priors = TRUE)

# Every family of relaxations, tested from this one fit. Under "Fixed
# cells, freed", freeing DIFFUSION[eta2,eta1] has a small p-value, so the
# data are not consistent with a zero covariance.
st <- ctScoreTest(fit)
print(st)

# One family's table: each fixed cell with its test, and an estimate of
# the parameter if it were freed.
print(st$fixed$cells)

# Whether subject level covariates, here the time independent predictors
# in the data, predict any parameter. The joint test is over all
# parameters.
stc <- ctScoreTest(fit,
  covariates = ctsemtestdat[, c('id', 'TI1', 'TI2', 'TI3')])
print(stc$covariates$TI1$joint)
}
# }
